newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First keeps nervous markets guessing.
newsitem.headline: NZ First keeps nervous markets guessing.

text.p: Nationalist New Zealand First kept rival parties and nervous markets guessing on Tuesday as it agonised over its choice of coalition partner to end two months of political uncertainty.
The party's 17 MPs, all but four of them new to parliament, must decide whether to keep the conservative National Party in office or restore centre-left Labour to power after six years in opposition.
Over weeks of negotiation, NZ First leader Winston Peters has thrashed out separate secret deals with National and Labour to put before his party for a decision.
By 5.40 p.m. (0440 GMT), more than seven hours after the meeting began, there was still no word on the timing and form of any announcement.
Shares closed slightly lower and bond yields crept higher at the close as the market began to lose its nerve. The New Zealand dollar slipped in thin, jittery trading.
Senior negotiators from both National and Labour made their way at intervals to the NZ First meeting room to clarify various points of detail.

Peters, the party's dominant figure, told reporters he would not express a personal preference and would let the caucus of MPs decide. "It's going to be a party and caucus decision...They will make the decision themselves," he said.
Peters formed NZ First after being sacked from cabinet by Prime Minister Jim Bolger in 1991, but says he will not allow bad blood to influence the choice.
NZ First won all five seats reserved for Maoris -- previously a stronghold of the Labour Party -- in the October 12 election. The Maori influence is crucial to the party's choice.
"Yes, my people have an expectation of me to go Labour," said Tutekawa Wyllie, MP for one of the Maori seats.

Another, Tukuroirangi Morgan, told reporters thousands of people in his constituency had deserted Labour for NZ First "because of the Labour Party's apathy and mediocrity. Maori people were sick and tired of being marginalised".

He added: "I've gone back to the people and they have said to me in some respects that the Labour Party is the preference but...it's an even race. We'll weigh up the decision on what will benefit Maori."
Maoris, who represent 13 percent of the population, make up a disadvantaged socio-economic group with poorer health, lower life expectancy and higher unemployment than whites.
National has presided over strong economic growth but lost ground during the election campaign as Labour and other parties promised greater funding for health and education.
National's campaign was largely based on the promise of further tax cuts next year, but it may have to compromise on the timing to accommodate NZ First's spending priorities.

NZ First fought the election on an economic strategy of export-led growth and promises to put ordinary New Zealanders' interests above those of foreigners and big business. It favours a 24.9 percent limit on foreign holdings in strategic assets.
National has 44 seats in the new 120-member parliament and Labour 37, with New Zealand First on 17.
A Labour-NZ First coalition would need support from the left-wing Alliance, which confirmed on Tuesday it would back such a government on confidence issues.
